candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — gestational diabetes screening timing
candidate.educational_objective: Teach pregnant clients that routine gestational diabetes screening generally occurs at 24–28 weeks, with earlier diabetes evaluation when clinically indicated by risk factors or history.

options.A: Routine glucose screening is usually performed between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy; earlier testing may be indicated when risk factors raise concern for diabetes.
options.B: Screening is delayed until after delivery unless symptoms of hyperglycemia occur during pregnancy.
options.C: All pregnant clients are screened only in the first trimester, and testing is never repeated later in pregnancy.
options.D: Routine screening is offered only to clients with a family history of diabetes.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current ACOG patient guidance states that glucose screening for gestational diabetes is usually performed between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Testing may occur earlier in pregnancy when risk factors for diabetes are present or when the client had gestational diabetes previously. ACOG also distinguishes screening from confirmatory testing; an abnormal initial glucose screen may require an additional glucose test. B, C, and D incorrectly delay or restrict screening.
candidate.source_claim_supported: ACOG recommends routine gestational diabetes glucose screening around 24–28 weeks for pregnant clients without established diabetes, with earlier testing when risk factors or history warrant it; abnormal screening may require confirmatory testing rather than assuming one universal test sequence for every client.
candidate.source_document_title: Routine Tests During Pregnancy; Gestational Diabetes; Clinical Practice Update: Screening for Gestational and Pregestational Diabetes in Pregnancy and Postpartum
